newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian T-bill prices seen rising on rouble policy.
newsitem.headline: Russian T-bill prices seen rising on rouble policy.

text.p: Russian Treasury bill prices are likely to rise in coming days after the central bank said it would maintain its exchange rate policy and make it easier for foreigners to get their money out, analysts said on Tuesday.

The central bank said the guaranteed yield for non-residents holding government securities to maturity would be cut to 13 percent from 16 percent from December 5. But, from the same date, the minimum term for foreigners repatriating proceeds from government securities would be cut to two months from three.
Earlier, the bank said its "sloping corridor" exchange rate policy would be maintained in 1997 but that the rouble's decline against the dollar would slow in line with forecast inflation.
"I see a big impact on prices in the next week or so because of both these things," said Alliance-Menatep fixed income analyst Dmitry Falkovich.
Many non-residents were likely to buy now to lock in the 16-percent yield and then fix a two-month forward next week to repatriate the proceeds, he said.
Since mid-August, non-residents have been able to open special rouble accounts at designated Russian banks, use them to buy T-bills and government bonds at auctions and trade in the secondary market.
Non-residents can repatriate funds from these accounts only through forward and option deals with a minimum term.
The guaranteed yield applies only to securities bought at auction and held to maturity so foreigners who hold paper for longer or trade aggressively can lock in higher yields.
Russian officials have been keen to reduce the cost of borrowing, particularly T-bill yields, in line with inflation.
The average T-bill yield in rouble terms on Tuesday was 39.4 percent, down from 90-105 percent at the beginning of the year.
Central Bank Chairman Sergei Dubinin told a news conference the rouble would be in a range of 5,500-6,100 per dollar on January 1, 1997, falling to a 5,750-6,350 range by December 31.
This would mean a depreciation of 0.3-1.1 percent a month in 1997, after about one-two percent a month in the second half of this year.
United Investment Bank chief dealer Alexander Suchkov said the change in the corridor was expected. "But its lower angle will in 1997 push down government bond yields further."

United City Bank fixed income analyst Andrei Yashchenko said prices had already been rising steadily in recent weeks. "It can't continue to grow at such an impressive pace, but there is still space to grow."
Analysts said the further fall in yields was expected after the success last week of Russia's debut Eurobond, which was oversubscribed despite being increased in volume to $1 billion.
The bond was priced to yield a tight 345 basis points over U.S. treasuries, and Yashchenko said this made a revaluation of all Russian fixed income instruments necessary.
"Yields should converge, even taking into account currency risk, and 13 percent is still attractive for a country with the rating Russia has," said Falkovich.
However, analysts said that even at reduced yields, the market would remain attractive.
"The yield is still interesting for non-residents because in other East European countries, it is 10-12 percent," said Oleg Surkov, capital markets manager at MFK bank.
The International Monetary Fund has been pressing Russia to ease non-residents' access to the government securities market in order to cut rates and encourage investment.
